prohibited_recommendations: Do not assume the recent secondarily generalized seizure indicates idiopathic generalized epilepsy and prescribe valproate without evaluating for focal onset.
Do not perform LP without first excluding raised ICP or shunt malfunction.
Do not start carbamazepine without confirming there is no hyponatremia from prior meningitis sequelae.
required_recommendations: Recognize lip-smacking automatisms with subsequent secondary generalization as focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures of temporal-lobe origin.
Pursue video-EEG monitoring to confirm lateralization given complex remote history.
Obtain 3T MRI with epilepsy protocol to characterize hippocampal sclerosis and assess for residual sequelae of prior meningitis or shunt-related changes.
Initiate a first-line AED for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lacosamide, or lamotrigine), accounting for any baseline cognitive impairment.
Confirm VP shunt is functioning (imaging review) — exclude as proximate cause.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

Witnessed automatisms and prolonged post-ictal phase are not syncope.

key_clinical_evidence: Childhood CNS insult (perinatal meningitis) is a recognized cause of subsequent dual pathology with mesial temporal sclerosis.
Focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures still localize to a focal onset zone — typically temporal in patients with HS.
Shunt malfunction must be considered but is unlikely with stereotyped focal semiology and no signs of raised ICP.
Multiple risk factors warrant epileptologist referral and consideration of surgical evaluation if refractory.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.

July 2026 review applied end to end: routine EEG first when appropriate, staged sleep-deprived/ambulatory escalation, video only for event capture or tertiary evaluation, and continuous ICU EEG only for NCSE.

patient.history_present_illness: This 24-year-old right-handed male with a complex neurological history including neonatal pneumococcal meningitis, VP shunt placement, chronic left spastic hemiparesis, and prior cervical spinal surgery presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His mother reports that over the past two months, the patient has experienced at least three episodes of behavioral arrest during which he appears to stare blankly, becomes unresponsive to verbal commands, and exhibits rhythmic lip-smacking and fumbling hand movements with his right hand lasting approximately 60 to 90 seconds each. After these episodes, he appears confused and disoriented for 10 to 15 minutes, often unable to recall the event. The family initially attributed these episodes to daydreaming or inattention related to his baseline cognitive profile. Yesterday evening, while watching television, the patient was observed to suddenly stop speaking mid-sentence, develop a fixed stare to the right, and begin lip-smacking. This progressed over approximately 30 seconds to bilateral arm stiffening followed by generalized rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately two minutes. He was incontinent of urine during the event. Post-ictally, he was confused, somnolent, and had new right arm weakness that gradually improved over two hours. Emergency medical services were called and the patient was transported to the emergency department. He had no prior seizure history despite his complex neurological background. Over the preceding weeks, the patient has also complained of intermittent headaches, which his family attributed to stress at work, and a vague sensation of an unpleasant smell that no one else could perceive, occurring several times per week for approximately one month. He denies recent head trauma, fever, or illness. He has not started any new medications, and there have been no changes to his baclofen regimen. His mother notes that he has appeared more fatigued and irritable over the past several weeks, with subtle decline in his already limited reading ability.
